explanations: luna: The source section treats fruit as food and one kind of sustenance; this ayah says rain produces fruits as provision for people, making that everyday yield an explicit divine provision.

luna: The source section moves from food fruit to lasting reward; this ayah describes garden dwellers repeatedly receiving fruit and recognizing what was provided before, making repeated provision part of the afterlife image. | terra: The righteous are repeatedly provided fruit in the gardens and recognize it as provision, directly joining fruit to recompense.

luna: The source section identifies manna and quails as food God gave Israel; this ayah names them with cloud shade and the instruction to eat good things provided, showing the gift in its own wilderness setting. | terra: The Israelites are shaded, given manna and quails, and told to eat the good things provided to them; this is the named heavenly-food branch of م ن ن.

luna: The source section recalls manna and quails as provisions in Israel's wilderness story; this ayah adds water from the rock for each tribe and tells them to eat and drink from God's provision, another concrete form of sustenance in that same story.

luna: The source section names manna as food bestowed on Israel; in this continuation of the wilderness meal story, the people reject one food and ask for vegetables and lentils from the earth, reversing gratitude for a given provision. | terra: The recipients of manna reject one food and ask for earth-grown vegetables, exchanging what is better for what is lower; it exposes ingratitude within the heavenly-food scene.
terra: The House is made a place of return and security immediately before Abraham asks for the town's fruit provision.

luna: The source section links fruit with a secure city; Abraham's prayer in this ayah asks for both a secure town and fruits for its people, holding safety and food together in one request. | terra: Abraham asks that the town be secure and that its people be provided with fruits, exactly uniting the safe city and fruit-rizq.
terra: Fear, hunger, and loss of wealth and fruits are named as trials, forming the precise negative boundary of secure fruit-abundance.
terra: Believers are commanded to eat the good things God provided and to thank Him, matching the section's movement from food to grateful recognition.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss says oil could be given as travel provisions; this pilgrimage instruction tells people to take provisions and then names reverent fear as the best provision, connecting carried food to the section's turn from bodily sustenance toward moral return. | terra: Pilgrims are told to take provisions for the journey and then that the best provision is mindfulness, extending material travel-food toward a nonmaterial provision as the section does.

luna: The source section's fruit and oil are material yields and its ajr is a lasting return; this ayah makes a seed producing many ears the image for multiplied spending in God's way, joining harvest to reward.

luna: The source section labels manna as a divine food-gift and mamnūn as the word for uninterrupted reward; this ayah uses the same root in its distinct sense of reproaching recipients after spending, then promises the spenders their reward, clarifying the root's different senses around giving. | terra: Those who do not follow spending with مَنّ or injury have their reward with their Lord, joining the reproach sense of the root to a reward left unspoiled by it.

luna: The source section's oil dictionary branch includes provisions given to a group, and its closing image ties deeds to reward; following the spending passage in 2:262, this ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, setting a boundary on material giving.

luna: The source section labels M-N-N for manna as bestowed food and mamnūn for uninterrupted reward; this ayah uses the root in the distinct sense of reproach after charity and pictures rain stripping soil from a rock, so the gift and the growable yield can both be lost.

luna: The source section treats fruit as provision that leads to an enduring reward; this ayah compares sincere spending to a garden that yields twice its fruit after rain, using produce to make the reward-bearing act perceptible.

luna: The source section moves from fruit as provision to a reward that will not be cut off; this ayah asks about a date-and-grape garden with many fruits destroyed by a fiery whirlwind in its owner's old age, a precise image of vulnerable worldly yield. | terra: A fruit-bearing garden needed by an elderly owner with weak dependents is consumed by a fiery whirlwind, dramatizing the loss of sustaining produce.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss makes olive oil a food given as group provisions; this ayah explicitly joins spending good things earned and produce brought forth from earth, linking cultivated food to its distribution.

luna: The source section calls its fruits and manna forms of rizq; this ayah repeatedly shows Zakariya finding provision with Mary in the sanctuary and her saying it is from God, making unexpected provision concrete. | terra: Mary receives unexpected provision in the sanctuary, and the scene states that God provides without account.

luna: The source section repeatedly joins a secure sanctuary to fruit and provision; this ayah itself says whoever enters the Sacred House is safe, adding the sanctuary's own safety claim to that meeting. | terra: The House is linked with clear signs and safety for whoever enters it, reinforcing the sanctuary side of the safe-city provision image.

luna: The source section explicitly labels its q-w-m root gloss as what sustains and suffices; this ayah calls wealth a qiyām for people and says to provide from it food and clothing, giving that support a concrete material form. | terra: Property is called قِيَامًا and its holders must provide food and clothing from it, directly realizing the dictionary sense of sustenance that keeps people standing.

luna: The source section explicitly labels Q-W-M as the root behind what sustains a person; this ayah uses the related form qawwāmūn and grounds household responsibility partly in spending wealth, a specific maintenance sense distinct from the section's lexical gloss. | terra: The description of household maintainers as قَوَّامُونَ is explicitly tied to spending wealth, another q-w-m form in a material-support relation.
terra: Believers are told to eat the lawful good things God provided and remain mindful of Him, joining food, provision, and moral response.
terra: Sea game is made food and benefit for residents and travelers, giving a concrete Quranic form to provisions carried on a journey.

luna: The source section explicitly connects the q-w-m root to a means of livelihood and explains qiyāman li-n-nās as what supports people's living and return; this ayah calls the Sacred House a qiyām for people, anchoring that gloss in its Quranic wording. | terra: God makes the Kaaba and sacred rites قِيَامًا لِلنَّاسِ; this is the wording behind the section's claim that the sacred center sustains people's worldly life and return.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss pictures olive oil as table food and its prose also names manna as food from above; this ayah's disciples ask for a table sent down from heaven, meeting the table and heavenly-food strands in a distinct scene. | terra: The disciples ask whether a table can be sent down from heaven, opening a direct counterpart to the section's table and descending-food images.

luna: The source section joins ordinary food with provision from heaven; after the request in 5:112, this ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured, adding their reason for asking. | terra: They explain that they wish to eat from the heavenly table and gain reassurance and certainty.

luna: The source section's table-food and bestowed-provision strands meet here: 5:113 states the disciples' wish to eat, and this ayah has Jesus ask for a heavenly table as a feast for the first and last of them and a sign. | terra: Jesus asks for a table sent from heaven as a feast and sign, and calls God the best provider; it joins the section's table image with food descending from above.

luna: The source section shows a town losing provision after ingratitude; following the heavenly table request in 5:114, this ayah makes disbelief after the delivered meal a boundary with punishment. | terra: God promises to send the table but attaches an exceptional warning to denial afterward, marking responsibility that follows provision.
terra: The source definition says the fig is eaten رَطْبًا وَيَابِسًا; this ayah's different use of moist and dry encompasses both states among what is hidden yet fully known.

luna: The source section's named word is the olive; this rain-grown inventory includes olive and pomegranate, said to be alike and unlike, adding variety within the provision of fruit. | terra: Rain-grown vegetation includes olive and pomegranate, and the hearer is told to look at fruit as it forms and ripens.

luna: The source section treats olives and figs as edible produce; this ayah names olives among gardens, dates, grapes, and pomegranates, then tells people to eat at harvest and give its due, tying the produce to use and distribution. | terra: Olive and pomegranate stand among cultivated produce, followed by commands to eat their fruit and give its due at harvest.
luna: The source section joins fruit with rain-fed provision; this ayah describes rain-bearing clouds sent to dead land and fruit brought forth from it, a direct growth scene.

luna: The source section recalls fruit asked for in a barren valley; this ayah contrasts good land whose plants emerge by its Lord's permission with poor land yielding little, giving a specific fertile/barren boundary.

luna: The source section's secure, well-provided town turns through ingratitude into hunger and fear; this ayah gives the opposite boundary, saying belief and mindfulness would open blessings from heaven and earth to town-dwellers. | terra: Faith and mindfulness would open blessings from heaven and earth, while denial turns that abundance into seizure.
terra: Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and shortage of fruits so that they might take heed.

luna: The source section identifies manna and quails as bestowed food; this ayah again names both and tells Israel to eat the good things provided, placing the gift among God's provisions. | terra: In the wilderness provision scene, water, shade, manna, quails, and the command to eat good provision occur together.
terra: Rain makes the earth's growth luxuriant until its possessors feel secure, then it is made like a harvested field overnight.
terra: Every creature's provision is God's responsibility, making sustaining livelihood universal rather than confined to the foods named in the section.

luna: The source section uses mamnūn for an unending wage; this ayah describes the blessed people's gift as not cut off, a parallel account of an unbroken return. | terra: The blessed are given عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, a gift explicitly not cut off and thus a close semantic counterpart to inexhaustible reward.
terra: The seven green ears and seven dry ears echo the source definition's fresh/dry wording within the famine-and-provision story, though the objects are grain rather than figs.

luna: The source section's dictionary account describes oil as food provision; Joseph tells the people to sow for seven years and keep most of the harvest in its ears, a specific way of preparing produce as stored sustenance. | terra: Joseph orders years of sowing and preservation of grain in its ears, showing food deliberately stored to sustain people through scarcity.

luna: The source section contrasts abundant provision with its loss; following Joseph's storage plan in 12:47, this ayah says the hard years consume the saved harvest, the direct reversal of stored sustenance. | terra: The severe years consume what was stored, furnishing the famine side of the press-and-abundance scene completed in 12:49.

luna: The source section describes oil squeezed from olives; after 12:48's famine years consuming the stored harvest, this ayah promises rain and a year when people press produce. The ayah does not identify olives, so the link is the pressing of produce after scarcity. | terra: After famine comes a year of rain in which people press produce, supplying the Quran's clearest counterpart to the olive press evoked by the section.
terra: Joseph equips his brothers with their provisions and promises full measure, a concrete caravan scene of food supplied for travel.
terra: Joseph orders the travelers' merchandise returned to their saddlebags so they will recognize it at home and return, continuing the provisioned-caravan scene.
terra: Adjacent plots, vineyards, crops, and palms drink the same water yet differ in produce, sharpening the section's cited contrast between similar and dissimilar fruits.
terra: God expands and restricts provision, while delight in worldly life is judged slight beside the Hereafter.

luna: The source section turns perishable food into an image of reward without interruption; this description of the promised garden says its food is lasting, directly setting enduring provision beside its worldly kinds. | terra: The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, making lasting fruit itself an image of provision that does not cease.
terra: Gratitude is promised increase while ingratitude meets severe punishment, the relation enacted by the section's abundance-and-loss examples.

luna: The source section's named image is edible fruit as provision; here rain brings forth fruits as provision for people, directly joining the fruit image to rizq. | terra: God sends rain and thereby brings out fruits as provision, stating the causal line that the olive-growth passages exemplify.
terra: Abraham asks that this city be secure, supplying the safety half of the fruit-provision prayer in 14:37.

luna: The source section pairs safe dwelling and fruit provision; Abraham's prayer places his family in a barren valley and asks that they be provided fruits so they may give thanks, making provision a requested gift where cultivation is absent. | terra: Abraham asks for fruit provision for his family in an uncultivated valley beside the Sacred House so that they may give thanks.
terra: God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not themselves provide for.
terra: God's treasuries are inexhaustible while what is sent down comes in a known measure, clarifying source and measure within earthly provision.

luna: The source section's named olive provision appears in 16:11; this preceding ayah supplies the rainwater and trees that frame the following olive and fruit yield. | terra: The water sent from heaven supplies drink and grows the vegetation on which herds feed, opening the rain-to-olive sequence of 16:11.

luna: The source section identifies the olive by root ز ي ت and follows its oil as provision; this ayah places olives among the crops and fruits grown by rain, locating that provision in rain-fed growth. | terra: Rain is the means by which God grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit for people.

luna: The source section defines figs and olives as things eaten and traces oil as food; this ayah describes dates and grapes yielding drink and good provision, broadening the tree-food image while distinguishing good provision from another use. | terra: The fruits of palms and vines yield both an intoxicant and good provision, another case of fruit being processed into distinct human uses.
terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and patient deeds receive their reward; this states the temporal boundary behind the uncut wage.

luna: The source section itself draws on this reversal: the ayah moves from a secure, content town receiving ample provision from everywhere to ingratitude, then to the garment of hunger and fear. | terra: A secure, tranquil town receiving abundant provision from every place denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; this is the section's central reversal in full.

luna: The source section cites 16:112's town losing abundance through ingratitude; this ayah states the fitting response to provision—eat what God has provided and be grateful—so its own contribution is gratitude at the meal. | terra: After the parable of lost security and abundance, people are told to eat lawful good provision and thank God's favor.
terra: Human dignity, carriage over land and sea, and provision from good things occur together, linking the honored human form with sustaining gifts.

luna: The source section develops fruit as provision; this ayah opens a parable with two date-and-grape gardens and crops, setting a concrete scene of abundant livelihood. | terra: The garden parable begins with two vineyards surrounded by palms and crops, establishing the fruit wealth later destroyed.

luna: The source section's fruit image is one of harvested provision; following 18:32's two gardens, this ayah says each produced its yield and had a river, specifying their productivity. | terra: Both gardens yield all their fruit without failing and have a river between them, defining the abundance reversed in 18:42.

luna: The source section sets food and livelihood beside an enduring reward; after the productive gardens in 18:33, this ayah describes their owner boasting of abundant fruit and wealth, exposing confidence in material provision.

luna: The source section reserves unendingness for the righteous wage; this ayah's garden owner assumes his orchard will never perish, a pointed contrast between imagined permanence of earthly fruit and the section's promised lasting return.

luna: After 18:35's claim that the garden will not perish, this ayah denies the Hour and expects an even better return; it makes the source section's distinction between worldly abundance and the afterlife reward concrete.
luna: The source section shows abundant provision vulnerable to reversal; this ayah warns that a garden's owner may wake to a calamity sent from heaven, directly placing crop security at risk.
luna: Following the threatened calamity in 18:40, this ayah names the garden's water sinking away; it identifies the loss of the source that sustains fruit-bearing land.

luna: The source section links fruit and provision with their possible loss; after 18:41's water disappears, this ayah says the garden's fruit is surrounded and its owner regrets his association, completing the reversal. | terra: The garden owner's fruit is destroyed and he wrings his hands over the collapsed trellises, a concrete reversal of fruit as secure wealth.

luna: The source section moves from perishable food to an unending reward; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that later dries and scatters, immediately before 18:46 names lasting good deeds. | terra: Worldly life is vegetation raised by rain and then scattered dry by the wind, setting edible growth within impermanence.

luna: The source section turns material provision into a comparison with lasting reward; this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment and the remaining good deeds better in reward and hope, stating that boundary in its own terms. | terra: After the vegetation image, lasting good deeds are declared better with the Lord in reward and hope.

luna: The source section's dictionary branch includes oil as provisions for a group; during their journey, Moses asks his companion for their lunch after travel fatigue, a specific carried meal in a travel scene.

luna: The source section treats fruit and oil as food provisions; this ayah supplies the stream immediately before 19:25's dates fall and 19:26's instruction to eat and drink, adding water to the meal scene.

luna: The source section treats fruit as edible provision; Mary is told to shake a palm trunk so fresh dates fall to her, a specific scene of fruit given for eating. | terra: Mary is told to shake the palm and receives fresh ripe dates, a direct Quranic scene of fresh fruit becoming immediate food.
luna: The source section joins food with sustenance; after the dates in 19:25, this ayah tells Mary to eat and drink and be comforted, completing the immediate meal scene.

luna: The source section says provision spans both worlds and calls the reward unending; this ayah describes the garden's people receiving provision morning and evening, a continuing afterlife supply.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss calls manna food God bestowed, and explicitly notes its meeting with the Tūr; this ayah names manna and quails after Israel's rescue and the promise at Tūr. | terra: At the promised meeting by the right side of the Mount, God sends down manna and quails, exactly joining the section's Tur setting to its heavenly food sense of م ن ن.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss presents manna as food God provided; following the manna in 20:80, this ayah tells Israel to eat the good things provided and warns against transgression, adding the required response to that food. | terra: Immediately after the manna and Mount scene, the recipients are told to eat the good things provided and not transgress in them.
terra: Adam is promised that in the Garden he will neither hunger nor be unclothed, defining sustenance by the needs it continuously removes.
terra: The Garden also protects Adam from thirst and exposure to the sun, completing the picture of provision that keeps a human being whole.

luna: The source section moves from worldly food and livelihood to an unending wage; this ayah calls the Lord's provision better and more lasting than the worldly life's adornment, making the time-bound/lasting distinction explicit. | terra: The passing bloom of worldly life is set against the Lord's provision, which is better and more lasting.

luna: The source section names the rain-grown olive in 23:20's food-and-oil scene; this immediately preceding ayah says water is sent down and stored in earth, while 23:19–20 supply the gardens and oil it enables. | terra: Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, beginning the sequence that culminates in edible gardens and the Sinai oil tree.

luna: The source section moves from edible fruit to food that sustains; this ayah grows date palms and grapevines into gardens with abundant fruits for people to eat, a parallel form of food-bearing provision. | terra: Rainwater produces palm-and-grape gardens with many fruits to eat, immediately before the Sinai oil tree.

luna: The source section's dictionary branch defines olive oil as an extract and as a food condiment; this ayah itself joins a tree from Sinai that grows oil with relish for eaters, making the oil both yield and food. | terra: The tree from Mount Sinai produces oil and a relish for eaters; it uniquely joins the surah's olive, its food and oil uses, and the adjacent Mount.

luna: The source section moves from edible provision to the reward for righteous deeds; this address to messengers places eating good things and acting righteously in the same command, joining nourishment and conduct without equating food with reward. | terra: The messengers are commanded to eat good things and do righteous deeds, directly linking food to the deeds that receive the section's unending reward.

luna: The source section names olive oil as a use of the olive; here oil from a blessed olive tree nearly shines without fire, extending the food-bearing tree into the surah's distinct image of light. | terra: The light parable names a blessed olive tree and oil that almost shines before fire touches it, developing the section's non-food use of pressed olive oil.
terra: The section's dictionary note names an olive-oil presser and seller; this immediate neighbour to the olive-lamp ayah mentions trade and sale, although it does not identify the goods as oil.
terra: In the continuation of the olive-light passage, God rewards deeds and gives provision without account, bringing light, reward, and boundless provision into one context.
terra: Spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but قَوَامًا between them, applying the q-w-m idea to a measure of expenditure that sustains life.
terra: Abraham names God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, identifying the giver behind every form of sustenance.
terra: The hearer is asked who sends rain and grows splendid gardens whose trees humans could not grow themselves.

luna: The source section joins safety with fruit provision; this ayah asks whether the people were established in a secure sanctuary to which fruits from every kind of place are brought. | terra: A secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every kind are gathered is presented as provision from God.

luna: The source section pairs a safe sanctuary with gathered fruits in 28:57; this next ayah recalls towns that exulted in their livelihood and were destroyed, putting a boundary around confidence in abundant provision.
luna: The source section ends its food-and-livelihood line with reward that does not end; this ayah says worldly gifts are enjoyment and adornment while what is with God is better and more lasting.
terra: People are commanded to seek provision from God, worship and thank Him, and are reminded that they return to Him; worldly maintenance and return are held together.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss pictures oil given as travel provisions; this ayah distinguishes creatures that carry no provision from God's provision for them and for people, sharpening the contrast between carried caravan food and sustenance supplied without being carried.

luna: The source section links a secure sanctuary with fruit brought from every place in 28:57; this ayah says the Haram is made safe while people nearby are seized, giving the boundary of security around that provision scene. | terra: A secure sanctuary amid people being snatched away is followed by the charge that its inhabitants deny God's favor.

luna: The source section's produce is food and provision; this ayah describes Sheba's two gardens and commands their people to eat their Lord's provision and give thanks, directly joining fruit, livelihood, and response. | terra: Saba's two gardens accompany the command to eat the Lord's provision and give thanks in a good land.

luna: Following 34:15's two gardens and grateful provision, this ayah says a flood changed them into bitter, sparse gardens, a direct reversal of abundant edible yield. | terra: When Saba turns away, its two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter produce, directly reversing the provision and gratitude of 34:15.

luna: After the garden loss in 34:16, this ayah names ingratitude as the reason for the repayment, completing the provision-and-response pattern also developed in the source section. | terra: The ruined gardens are identified as repayment for ingratitude, making explicit why the provision of 34:15 was reversed.
terra: Between Saba and the blessed towns, God placed visible settlements and measured stages, telling the people to travel through them safely by night and day.
terra: The people ask that their journeys be lengthened, wrong themselves, and are scattered, reversing the safe and measured travel provision of 34:18.
terra: God expands and restricts provision, replaces whatever is spent, and is called the best provider.
terra: Water sent from heaven brings forth fruits of varied colors, a direct rain-to-fruit parallel to the olive passages.
luna: The source section moves from worldly food and provision to unending reward; this ayah joins spending from what God provided with hope for a trade that will never fail.

luna: The source section calls the wage an enduring form of provision; following 35:29's spending and unfailing trade, this ayah says God will repay the workers fully and increase them from His grace.

luna: The source section treats the olive and other fruit as nourishment; this ayah points to dead earth revived and grain from it as food, connecting provision to the land's renewal. | terra: Revived dead earth produces grain from which people eat, opening a rain-and-food sequence parallel to the olive catalogues.

luna: Following the grain from dead earth in 36:33, this ayah names date palms and grapes with springs, extending the edible growth scene. | terra: Palm and grape gardens with springs supply the immediate setting for eating their fruit.

luna: The source section describes fruit as an eaten gift; after the gardens in 36:34, this ayah names their fruit for people to eat and raises the question of gratitude for what they did not make. | terra: People eat the fruit of the gardens while being reminded that their hands did not create it and asked whether they will give thanks.

luna: The source section treats fruit as food and sustenance; this ayah promises fruit to the garden's people and adds that they have what they ask, making the supply part of their recompense. | terra: The people of Paradise have fruit and whatever they request, a concise fruit-as-reward scene.
terra: God brings fire from a green tree, a close counterpart to olive oil becoming light and to fuel supplied from a tree.

luna: The source section calls its fruit, oil, and manna forms of rizq and links rizq to reward; 37:42 names fruit for the people of 37:41's known provision, while this ayah supplies that provision frame. | terra: The sincere servants are promised a known provision, which the next ayah specifies as fruits.

luna: The source section treats fruit as food and as the start of a line toward reward; following 37:41's known provision, this ayah names fruit and honor for the recipients. | terra: Fruits are the named form of the honored provision promised in the preceding ayah.
luna: The source section connects material provision to an enduring reward; 37:42 names the fruit, and 37:43 itself locates its recipients in gardens of bliss.
terra: God says He bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron, a m-n-n use of divine favor in the same Mosaic setting as manna and the Mount.
terra: Solomon is told that God's gift is his to bestow, فَامْنُنْ, or withhold without account; the ayah joins the m-n-n gift sense to abundance without reckoning.
terra: The inhabitants of Eden call for abundant fruit and drink, supplying the concrete feast later described in 38:54 as provision without depletion.
terra: Paradise is called God's provision and is said to have no depletion, stating directly the section's reading of unending reward as inexhaustible rizq.
terra: The steadfast are paid their reward without account, a close formulation of reward without a limiting measure.

luna: The source section calls the continuing wage a form of provision; this ayah joins entry into the Garden for good deeds with being provided there without reckoning. | terra: The righteous enter the Garden and are provided there without account, explicitly construing eschatological reward as unlimited provision.
terra: God gives the earth as settlement, forms human beings well, and provides good things, bringing excellent human formation and sustenance into one ayah.

luna: The source section quotes mamnūn for reward that does not run out; this ayah repeats أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ for believers who do good, directly showing the same reward wording elsewhere. | terra: Belief and good works receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, an exact parallel to the section's unceasing wage.
terra: The afterlife and worldly aims are figured as two harvests; the first is increased while the second leaves no share in the Hereafter.

luna: The source section's q-w-m gloss is sustenance that keeps a person standing and suffices; this ayah says provision is sent in measure, since unrestricted abundance would cause transgression, making sufficiency and limit explicit.

luna: The source section distinguishes worldly forms of sustenance from an enduring wage; this ayah calls what people receive in this life enjoyment and says what is with God is better and lasting for believers.
terra: God apportions people's livelihood in worldly life, making sustenance a distributed measure rather than a self-produced possession.

luna: The source section identifies fruit as edible provision; this ayah tells garden dwellers they have abundant fruits from which they eat, giving the afterlife counterpart. | terra: Abundant fruit in Paradise is given for its inhabitants to eat, treating fruit as continuing eschatological provision.
terra: The people of Paradise call there for every kind of fruit while secure, joining fruit, safety, and final provision in one scene.

luna: The source section extends fruit and oil into the idea of sustained provision; this garden description includes fruits among its promised provisions, alongside rivers of several kinds. | terra: The promised Garden contains every kind of fruit together with forgiveness, another explicit meeting of fruit and final recompense.
terra: Some people count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, while the ayah says God favors them by guidance; this clarifies human reproach versus divine favor within the m-n-n root.

luna: The source section locates fruit and oil within provision; this ayah starts a rain scene with blessed water and gardens and harvested grain, setting up the provision named in 50:11. | terra: Blessed rain from heaven grows gardens and harvest grain, beginning the passage that calls these foods provision.

luna: After 50:9's rain and gardens, this ayah adds tall date palms with clustered fruit, a concrete food-bearing tree before the provision conclusion. | terra: Tall palms with layered clusters supply the fruit detail before the passage names provision.

luna: The source section names fruit and food as rizq; following the rain, grain, and date palms in 50:9–10, this ayah identifies them as provision for servants and evidence of revival. | terra: The rain-grown grain and palms are provision for servants, and the same scene turns to resurrection from dead land.

luna: The source section says provision reaches across two worlds and joins material rizq to promised reward; this ayah itself pairs provision in heaven with what people are promised. | terra: Provision and what is promised are said to be in heaven, directly illuminating the section's heavenly food and promised wage.

luna: The source section makes reward the continuing form of provision; this ayah tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did, explicitly making food part of recompense. | terra: The people of the Garden are told to eat and drink for what they used to do, explicitly identifying the meal as recompense.

luna: The source section treats fruit as a kind of provision and reward as its enduring form; this ayah says the garden's people are supplied with fruit and meat, a concrete afterlife provision. | terra: God continually supplies the Garden's people with fruit and meat they desire, completing the reward-meal of the passage.

luna: The source section treats fruit as food and provision; this ayah names fruit and date clusters in the earth-garden scene, giving specific produce rather than an abstract blessing. | terra: The earth is described as bearing fruit and date palms, another direct catalogue of edible gifts.

luna: After the fruit and date clusters in 55:11, this ayah adds grain with husk and fragrant plants, expanding the scene to staple food and edible growth. | terra: Husked grain and fragrant plants accompany the fruit and palms of the preceding ayah, completing a table of earth-grown provision.
terra: The two gardens contain two kinds of every fruit, presenting fruit as abundant final provision.
terra: Fruit, palms, and pomegranates occur together in the later pair of gardens, recalling the produce catalogues in which olive and pomegranate are paired.

luna: The source section treats fruit as edible provision that leads toward enduring reward; this ayah specifies fruits the Garden's people choose, a concrete instance of that provision. | terra: Chosen fruit forms part of the served banquet of the foremost, another meeting of fruit and eschatological reward.
terra: Abundant fruit is one item of the provision of the companions of the right.

luna: The source section connects fruit to ajr ghayr mamnūn; this ayah describes garden fruit as neither cut off nor withheld, a specific unbroken supply of the same food the section begins with. | terra: That fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, making fruit the direct form of the section's uninterrupted provision.
terra: The hearer is asked to consider the fire people kindle, opening the tree-and-traveler benefit completed in 56:72-73.
terra: The question asks whether people produced the fire's tree or God did, supplying the tree source for the travelers' benefit of the next ayah.
terra: Fire is made a reminder and a benefit for desert travelers, echoing both the olive oil's light-use and the section's caravan provision, though the fuel tree is not identified as olive.

luna: The source section contrasts edible worldly yield with an unending wage; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown plants that later yellow and crumble, making the perishing side of that contrast visible. | terra: Worldly growth pleases its cultivators, then yellows and crumbles, while the ayah turns to forgiveness and divine pleasure in the Hereafter.
terra: Whoever is mindful of God is provided for from an unexpected source, and reliance rests on God's fulfillment and measured ordering.
terra: Spending is scaled to the provision one has received, and restricted provision still carries a command to spend from God's gift.

luna: The source section's dictionary entry depicts oil packed as provisions for a traveling group; this ayah joins walking over the earth with eating God's provision, a specific pairing of travel and food. | terra: People are told to travel through the made-manageable earth, eat God's provision, and remember resurrection to Him, closely joining journey-food, livelihood, and return.
terra: Immediately after the command to eat provision from the earth, the hearer is asked whether he feels secure from that earth swallowing him.
terra: The provision scene is further bounded by the question whether anyone is secure from a stone-bearing wind.

luna: The source section quotes mamnūn for reward without end; this ayah gives the Prophet an ajr ghayr mamnūn, extending the same wording to a different addressee. | terra: The Prophet is promised أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ, preserving the section's phrase for reward that is never cut off.
terra: The owners of a garden who swear to harvest it are presented as a trial, opening a reversal of confidence in produce.
terra: A visitation from the Lord strikes the garden while its owners sleep, removing the crop they assumed they controlled.
terra: The garden owners resolve to exclude the poor from the harvest, reversing the command to give produce its due at harvest in 6:141.
terra: After the crop's loss and their confession, the owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better.
terra: The fruit clusters of the lofty Garden are brought near to the recipient of the record in his right hand.

luna: The source section joins righteous deeds to an enduring wage; this ayah tells the Garden's people to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they sent ahead, directly connecting nourishment with earned return. | terra: The blessed are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead, explicitly naming the meal as recompense.

terra: The wording can mean not to confer a favor seeking increase; on that reading it contrasts interested human giving with the section's unceasing divine reward, though the verb's interpretation is disputed.

luna: The source section's dictionary entry pictures oil as provisions for a group and its surah grants reward for righteous deeds; this ayah describes the righteous giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it.

luna: The source section moves from food to reward; after 76:8's feeding of others, this ayah says the givers seek God's face and want neither reward nor thanks from recipients, clarifying the relation between provision and recompense.

luna: The source section moves from fruit as worldly food to an enduring wage; this ayah describes the Garden's shade and fruit made near, a specific food provision within the reward scene. | terra: The Garden's fruit clusters are brought within easy reach, making fruit a readily available reward rather than a failing supply.
luna: The source section calls the wage an unending provision; after 76:8–14's giving and Garden scene, this ayah itself identifies the outcome as their reward and their effort as appreciated.

luna: The source section treats fruit as provision and the righteous wage as its lasting counterpart; this ayah names desired fruits among the Garden's gifts that 77:43 then identifies with recompense. | terra: The mindful receive the fruits they desire.

luna: The source section ties righteous deeds to reward; after 77:42's fruit, this ayah tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did. | terra: They are told to eat and drink in satisfaction because of what they used to do.
terra: The passage identifies that food as God's recompense for those who do good.
terra: Gardens and grapevines are the first concrete items in the reward promised to the mindful in the preceding ayah.

luna: The source section's wording explicitly pairs the human and the olive through 80:24 and 80:29; this ayah itself commands a person to consider his food, turning the meal into an inquiry developed by the following crop sequence. | terra: The command that the human being look at his food opens the very food sequence in which the section locates the olive.

luna: The source section's food image is explicitly paired with the olive in 80:24 and 80:29; 80:24 sets the food question, and 80:25 itself supplies the poured water that begins the sequence explaining its source. | terra: The food inspection is unpacked first as God's abundant pouring of water.

luna: After 80:25's poured water, this ayah contributes the earth being split, the stage before the crops named in 80:27–31 and the provision identified in 80:32. | terra: The earth is then split open, the physical act that makes the food list possible.

luna: After 80:26 opens the earth, this ayah names grain as the first crop in the sequence that ends with provision in 80:32, adding a direct food crop. | terra: Grain is the first food grown in the sequence that later names olive.

luna: Following grain in 80:27, this ayah names grapes and green fodder; the source section's edible fruit and provisions image makes these another concrete crop and animal food. | terra: Grapes and fresh herbage broaden the foods surrounding olive in the same catalogue.

luna: The source section explicitly notes its human-and-olive pairing with this ayah; 80:29 itself names olives and date palms among the crops, locating the olive in a human food sequence. | terra: Olive and palm are explicitly items in the food catalogue begun by the command to look at one's food.

luna: After 80:29's olives and date palms, this ayah adds dense gardens to the food-growing scene that 80:32 calls provision for people and livestock. | terra: Dense gardens provide the cultivated setting for the food list.

luna: The source section identifies fruit as food; after the gardens in 80:30, this ayah names fruit and pasture before 80:32 identifies the sequence as provision. | terra: Fruit and pasture gather human food and animal feed in the same provision scene.

luna: The source section's dictionary entry describes oil as provision given to a group; 80:31 names fruit and fodder, and 80:32 itself identifies the sequence as provision/enjoyment for people and livestock. | terra: The catalogue is identified as provision for people and their livestock.

luna: The source section quotes mamnūn for uninterrupted reward; this ayah gives believers who do good the same ajr ghayr mamnūn, pairing the phrase with faith and action as in the section. | terra: The exception for believers who do good ends with أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, repeating both the condition and reward of 95:6.

luna: The source section moves from earthly food to reward without end; 87:17 says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, while this ayah supplies the contrasted preference for the nearer life. | terra: People prefer the nearer life, the transient side of the section's two-world provision.

luna: Following 87:16's preference for the nearer life, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, a direct boundary for the source section's move from ordinary provision to unending reward. | terra: The Hereafter is better and more lasting, completing the boundary introduced by preference for the nearer life.
terra: Quraysh's settled covenant or accustomed security opens the short passage that joins caravan journeys to feeding and safety.
terra: The winter and summer caravan journeys supply the travel setting for the food and security named two ayat later.
terra: The command to worship the Lord of this House identifies the giver and sanctuary behind Quraysh's food and safety.

luna: The source section links a community's food and security; this ayah itself joins being fed against hunger with being made safe from fear, and 106:2 supplies the chapter's seasonal travel setting. | terra: The Lord of the House feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, the same food-and-safety pairing developed by the section.
